messages.author: 38e260fc5780b4d6
messages.subject: specifying a gradient function
parts:
Hi Stan team,

I am trying to implement my own gradient function, but figured I'd check with you Stan folk in case someone has ideas about this or has already done it. Upon tracing an existing model I see that stan/gm/command.hpp:434 calls log_prob_grad (stan/model/util.hpp:168) which appears to set up the auto diff infrastructure and calls my model log_prob function. To call my own log_prob_grad functions, should I modify the log_prob_grad function in util.hpp? 

I'm running the git dev version.

Cheers,
Andria

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] specifying a gradient function
parts:
Hi Andria,

First off -- sorry, we haven't documented how to write in your own derivatives. It's going to take a little work, but if you have all the analytic gradients, that's awesome and we can help you implement it directly.

No, you don't want to touch src/stan/gm/command.hpp. What you want to do is edit the generated code. If you're Stan model is in foo.stan, the place to look is foo.cpp. You can generate that directly by typing:
   make foo.cpp

That will pass the Stan file through bin/stanc, the Stan parser and code generator. Inside the foo.cpp file, you want to look and edit the ```log_prob(...)` function. If you make any changes and want to compile the edited model, you'll just type:
    make foo
or in Windows
    make foo.exe

So that leaves how to edit the log_prob function. It isn't natural, but if you want to add hand coded gradients, it will be labeled as the model block within the generated C++ code. I'll try to outpline in the Bastille.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] specifying a gradient function
parts:
Hi Daniel,

Just to confirm, my goal is to write a function in C++ that computes both the log probability and its gradient in one shot, without using any auto-differentiation.

I think I left out some details from my first post.  I used stanc to generate a .cpp file from the .stan file.  Within the generated .cpp file there is a function called log_prob that unpacks parameters and executes the model block from the stan file.  I noticed that a vector for storing the gradient is not passed to this log_prob function.  After further inspection I noticed that this log_prob function is called from the log_prob_grad function in util.hpp, and that log_prob_grad is passed a vector for storing the gradient.  The log_prob_grad function sets up some auto-diff stuff before calling log_prob (in the generated .cpp file) and this is used to fill the gradient vector.

I didn't see any code in util.hpp that looks/tests for a user supplied log_prob_grad function, so I figured that I could just replace the body of the log_prob_grad function in util.hpp with a call to my own C++ routine that would fill the gradient vector manually...

Thanks,
Andria

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] specifying a gradient function
parts:
Daniel,

I think things have changed with how the generated models work now.  log_prob_grad is a static function which explicitly uses the autodiff variable type to call the (generated) log_prob function.  I'm not sure when this change was made exactly or why, but it makes it much more complicated for a user (like Andria) to implement a custom model and gradients in C++.  The instructions used to be as simple as "gut and reimplement log_prob and overload log_prob_grad in your generated model."

Andria,

You need to implement a template specialization of the function log_prob_grad for your specific model as well as changing your models log_prob function.  To do this you don't need to modify util.hpp, but rather you just need to write your own version of log_prob_grad in the generated C++ file but restricted to M being your specific model class.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] specifying a gradient function
parts:
You probably want to start with a Stan model and use
that to generate a skeleton implementation of a model.
You'll need it to implement all the I/O functions.

You want to define appropriate constraints on parameters
and leave the initial part of the log probability (and
other) functions that deal with the transforms, including
the Jacobian adjustments.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] specifying a gradient function
parts:
[back on stan-users list]

That's true not just for the distributions, but for all
functions. You can specify the template instantiation
to double if you want, and it'll skip the derivatives.

You are going to have to pull the double values out
of the input agrad values to operate on.

Have you already figured out how to construct the
agrad value for the result based on the agrads of
the inputs so it gets percolated?

As I said to the last poster who asked, it might be
easier to just write a function that computes the
derivatives and then plug that into the model directly
rather than trying to manipulate the generated code,
which is going to be hard to maintain under any minor
changes.

- Bob

> use of the stan distributions. I think the appearance of agrad in there means I need to avoid using these distributions
> in my manual lp and grad code - is this correct?
>
> Thanks so much for all your help!
> Andria

> On 10 January 2014 02:38, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:

>

> On 1/10/14, 6:16 AM, Andria Dawson wrote:
>
> Thanks so much for the instructions and tips. With some help from others (that are more experienced with
> C++) I have
> made some progress with specializing log_prob_grad, but do have a few questions as I move forward...
>
> 1. There seem to be two versions of log_prob_grad (in util.hpp), one with real and integer parameters, and
> one with only
> real parameters. Do I need to specialize both, or is only one used by NUTS?
>
>
> No -- the one without integer parameters calls the other one, so
> you should be able to leave that as is. We'll be continuing to
> refine the model structure. We're dropping integer parameters because
> we've never gotten around to implementing them and don't have any
> short-term plans to do so (the problem remains figuring out the Markov
> blanket of an integer parameter in order to easily do Gibbs sampling).
>
> 2. Is log_prob_propto (in util.hpp) used in NUTS?
>
>
> Not as far as I know. We put that in for optimization. And it
> should also just be calling the basic log_prob function, so shouldn't
> need to be specialized.
>
> 3. Are there any other functions used by NUTS that use automatic differentiation that I need to be aware of?
>
>
> The variable transforms do, but there's no good way to specialize
> this unless you define all your parameters on an unconstrained scale
> and do the transforms yourself.
>
> - Bob
>
>
